summary.text: The Byzantine Empire, also called the Eastern Roman Empire, was the continuation of the Eastern part of the Roman Empire, centred on Constantinople.
It survived the fall of the Western Roman Empire in the 5th century and lasted until Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Empire in 1453.
Its own citizens called it the Roman Empire and themselves Romans, because the name Byzantine was coined only after it ended.

facts.label: Greatest extent
facts.value: Under Justinian I, who briefly reconquered much of Italy

facts.label: What citizens said
facts.value: They called themselves Romans, not Byzantines

facts.label: End
facts.value: Fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans in 1453

items.prompt: A citizen of the empire hears a scholar call his state the "Byzantine Empire". Why would that name puzzle him?

options.label: He thought of himself as a Greek, not a Roman
Byzantine was a title kept for the emperor alone
The name was coined only after his empire was gone
His empire was known only as the Eastern Empire

items.explain: The term Byzantine Empire was coined only after the empire's demise. Its citizens used the term Roman Empire and called themselves Romans.

items.prompt: Constantine wanted a new capital instead of ruling from Rome. Which reason does the account give?

options.label: Rome was far from the rich eastern provinces and less strategic
Rome's people refused to accept his favour for Christianity
Rome had been left in ruins by the Goths
Rome was too small to hold a growing court

items.explain: Rome was farther from the prosperous eastern provinces and in a less strategically important location, so Constantine rebuilt the city of Byzantium as a new capital.

items.prompt: A student charts the empire's fortunes and sees it lose land, regain strength, and then lose land again. Which description fits best?

options.label: Steady growth that ended in one sudden collapse
Steady decline from Justinian's reign onward
One long fall after the empire was first divided
Recurring cycles of decline and recovery

items.explain: After adopting a defensive strategy, the empire went through recurring cycles of decline and recovery, such as stabilising under the Isaurian dynasty and expanding under the Macedonian dynasty.

items.prompt: Justinian I had briefly reconquered much of the western Mediterranean coast. Why did the decades after his reign bring political and strategic challenges?

options.label: The Fourth Crusade broke the empire into rival states
A plague and a long war with Persia strained its money and army
The Ottomans annexed its remaining territories in a series of wars
Diocletian's Tetrarchy split the empire in two

items.explain: A plague began around 541 and prolonged warfare with Persia placed fiscal and military strain on the empire. The Fourth Crusade and the Ottoman wars came centuries later.

items.prompt: Constantinople was sacked in the Fourth Crusade and retaken in 1261. How strong was the restored empire?

options.label: It ruled the eastern Mediterranean as before
It stayed split between Greek and Latin realms
It held only regional power in its last two centuries
It became a vassal state of the Western emperors

items.explain: Despite the recovery of Constantinople, the reconstituted empire wielded only regional power during its final two centuries, until the Ottomans ended it in 1453.

items.prompt: After 800, a German emperor's court calls the eastern empire "the Greeks". What is behind that choice of label?

options.label: Its people called themselves Graeci
The Western court claimed to be the true heirs of Roman identity
Greek had replaced Latin as the language of the West
It matched what Islamic neighbours called the empire

items.explain: After 800, Western Europe called them Greeks because the Papacy and medieval German emperors regarded themselves as the true inheritors of Roman identity. The empire's own people saw themselves as Romans.

paragraphs.heading: Rome's eastern half lives on
paragraphs.text: The Byzantine Empire, also called the Eastern Roman Empire, was the eastern part of the Roman Empire carrying on through late antiquity and the Middle Ages, with Constantinople as its centre. It outlasted the fall of the western half in the 5th century AD and kept going until the Ottoman Empire took Constantinople in 1453. The name Byzantine was only invented after the empire was gone. Its own people spoke of the Roman Empire and thought of themselves as Romans.

paragraphs.heading: Splitting the empire
paragraphs.text: In the 3rd century AD the Roman Empire was hit by outside threats and inner crises, and regional armies began naming their own generals emperor. One of these, Diocletian, decided the state was too large for one ruler. He set up the Tetrarchy, a system that split the empire into an eastern and a western half. The system soon collapsed, but the idea of a divided empire stuck.

paragraphs.heading: A new capital in the east
paragraphs.text: Constantine I won absolute power in 324. Over the following six years he rebuilt the town of Byzantium as a new capital he called "New Rome", later named Constantinople. He made Christianity legal, reformed the army and government, and introduced a stable gold coin, the solidus. Under Theodosius I, Christianity became the state religion, and over time Greek took the place of Latin in official business.

paragraphs.heading: Greatest reach and great losses
paragraphs.text: The empire was at its largest under Justinian I, who reigned from 527 to 565 and for a time won back much of Italy and the western Mediterranean coast. A plague that started around 541 and long wars with Persia then strained its money and armies. In the 630s and 640s Arab armies beat Byzantine forces in Syria and Egypt, and those provinces were lost for good. Africa followed in 698.

paragraphs.heading: Revival and fall
paragraphs.text: The empire steadied under the Isaurian dynasty and grew again under the Macedonian dynasty, enjoying a two-century renaissance. Civil wars and Seljuk raids later cost it most of Asia Minor, but it recovered in the Komnenian restoration. Constantinople stayed Europe's biggest and richest city until Paris passed it in the 13th century. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople and broke the empire into pieces. The city was retaken in 1261, but the empire was only a regional power after that, and the Ottomans swallowed what was left until Constantinople fell in 1453.

paragraphs.heading: Romans, Greeks or Byzantines
paragraphs.text: Its people called themselves Romaioi, Romans, and their Muslim neighbours called the empire the "land of the Romans". After 800 AD, Western Europe called them Greeks instead, because the Pope and the medieval German emperors claimed to be Rome's true heirs. The word Byzantine comes from Byzantion, the Greek settlement on which Constantinople was built, and at first it described only the city's people. It is now the main term for the empire, though some modern historians say it should be dropped as unfair and inaccurate in origin.
